title: Past, present, future mind (section 18)
hookLine: past mind can't be grasped, present mind can't be grasped, future mind can't be grasped

cards: A story told in the Zen tradition: a learned monk is on the road, his pack full of his own commentaries on the Diamond Sutra. Hungry, he stops at a roadside stall to buy a snack from an old woman.
She asks what's in the pack. Notes on the Diamond Sutra, he says. I have a question, she says.
Answer it, and the snack is free. The sutra says past mind can't be grasped, present mind can't be grasped, future mind can't be grasped. So which mind is this snack for?
He has no answer. Today, the line she quoted.

teach.b: First, the eyes. Section eighteen opens with short questions. Does the Tathagata have the physical eye?
He does, Subhuti says. The heavenly eye? The wisdom eye?
The eye of the teaching? The eye of a Buddha? Yes, to each.
Five ways of seeing, and the Buddha has every one. Second, the sand. Picture as many rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and as many worlds as there are grains in all those rivers.
All the beings in all those worlds, with all their kinds of minds, the Tathagata knows. Third, the turn. Then why does he know them?
Because, the sutra says, what are called minds are not minds; that is why they are called minds.
The Buddha who sees every mind sees that none is a fixed, solid thing.

Past mind can't be grasped: it's gone, and what's left is memory, happening now. Future mind can't be grasped: it isn't here yet, and what's here is planning, happening now. Present mind can't be grasped either.
Reach for it, and by the time your hand closes, it has moved. That's what silenced the monk. He had studied this line and written about it, but a snack is eaten now, and now can't be caught and held.
Some readers hear despair in that. The sutra seems to hear freedom.
A mind that can't be grasped also can't be trapped. Yesterday's mistake isn't a cell. Tomorrow's worry isn't a wall.
Even this moment's mood is already on its way.

how: The line about past, present and future mind is quoted in Chan and Zen teaching, and the story of the monk and the snack seller is told as a teaching tale about it.

o: the old days the sutra says were better than now
one of three minds the sutra says can't be grasped
an old mistake that stays with you forever

games.q: can't be grasped: tap the pairs.
p: asks which mind the snack is for

s: the sutra says only the past and future can't be grasped
present mind can't be grasped either.
section 18 says the Tathagata knows the minds of beings in countless worlds
as many worlds as grains of sand in as many Ganges rivers.
in the story, the monk's commentaries help him answer
he has no answer for the old woman.

games.q: you're the monk with a pack of commentaries. the snack seller asks: past, present and future mind can't be grasped, so which mind is this snack for? what do you do?
o: say the present mind, of course
games.why: in the story he has no answer; the line he had studied met him in a moment he couldn't hold.

practice: As a breath arrives, try to catch it, to hold this exact instant still, and notice what happens: it's already turning, already leaving.

Try again on the next one, without strain; the point isn't to succeed but to feel the moment slip through the fingers, and see whether that feels like loss or like room. When a memory or a plan pulls you away, let it go too.

wordCard.voice: Past. With present and future, one of the three minds the Diamond Sutra says can't be grasped. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: mind, heart-mind; section 18 says past, present and future mind can't be grasped.

carryVoice: Your line: can't be grasped. Not a cell, not a wall: room. A new week, begun.

sources.ref: Zen teaching story of the monk with his commentaries and the snack seller
